title: Ovary & Fallopian Tube Anatomy: Follicles, Ampulla, Map
description: Explore ovary and fallopian tube anatomy, covering the ovarian cortex, follicle stages, corpus luteum, fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus, and dual blood supplies.
h1: Ovary and Fallopian Tube (Uterine Tube) Anatomy: Follicles and Segments
blurb: Follicular waves and corpus luteum formation in the ovarian cortex paired with the fimbriae, wide ampulla, and ciliated mucosa of the fallopian tube.
lead: Paired on either side of the uterus, the ovaries and feather-tipped uterine tubes work in concert yet are not fused—requiring sweeping fimbriae to catch each ovulated egg. In this illustrated guide to ovary and fallopian tube anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including ovarian cortex, ovarian medulla, primordial follicles, growing follicles—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Paired on either side of the uterus, the ovaries and feather-tipped uterine tubes work in concert yet are not fused—requiring sweeping fimbriae to catch each ovulated egg. Follow the oocyte from dominant follicle across a peritoneal gap to the fimbriae and ampulla, then trace the tube to the uterine cornu. Within the human body, the ovary & uterine tube (Ovarium et tuba uterina) is situated in lateral pelvis / broad ligament, receives arterial perfusion via ovarian artery from aorta + tubal branches of uterine artery, and is innervated by ovarian and uterovaginal autonomic plexuses.

The ovarian cortex (Cortex ovarii) is outer ovarian zone with follicles at several stages. Physiologically, the ovarian cortex houses the oocyte reserve. The ovarian medulla (Medulla ovarii) is central vascular stromal zone. Physiologically, the ovarian medulla supports vessels, nerves and the hilum. The primordial follicles (Folliculi primordiales) are small oocyte with flat granulosa cells in outer cortex. Physiologically, the primordial follicles governs dormant ovarian reserve pool. Structurally, the growing follicles (Folliculi crescentes) comprises developing granulosa and theca layers, then antrum. Physiologically, the growing follicles governs estrogen synthesis and oocyte maturation. The dominant antral follicle (Folliculus maturus) is large fluid-filled preovulatory follicle. Physiologically, the dominant antral follicle releases a secondary oocyte after the LH surge. Structurally, the corpus luteum comprises yellow luteinized structure after ovulation. Physiologically, the corpus luteum produces progesterone during luteal phase.

Clinically, regarding the ovarian cortex, cortical tissue is considered in fertility-preserving surgery. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the ovarian medulla, ovarian pedicle bleeding arises at the hilum. In clinical pathology involving the primordial follicles, reserve declines with age and treatment exposure. Medical evaluation of the growing follicles also notes that follicle tracking uses size, not a diagnosis of oocyte quality.

questions.question: Where does an egg go after ovulation?
questions.answer: After release from an ovarian follicle, the oocyte is taken up near the fimbriae and usually enters the uterine tube before moving toward the uterus.

questions.question: Which part of the fallopian tube is the usual site of fertilization?
questions.answer: The ampulla, a wider segment of the uterine tube, is the most common site of fertilization.

questions.question: What is the ovarian cortex?
questions.answer: The ovarian cortex is the outer region of the ovary containing follicles at different stages of development.

questions.question: Where are the primordial follicles located?
questions.answer: Primordial follicles lie in the ovarian cortex and contain an oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular cells.

questions.question: What is the function of the dominant antral follicle?
questions.answer: After the luteinizing hormone surge, the dominant antral follicle releases a secondary oocyte at ovulation.
